components.name: Event bus (Kafka: notifications, settlement, fraud scoring)

monthly_cost_per_instance.measured_context: kafka.m5.large — AWS MSK us-east-1 / On-Demand / provisioned broker / 730 h per month; broker-hour only (excludes storage and data transfer). Band: zero-width: single published broker-hour rate in the pinned scope.

assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: 12,000 req/s peak. Split: 55% balance check, 20% transaction history, 18% P2P transfer, 7% top-up — a consumer wallet is read-dominated, with money movement a quarter of traffic.

assumptions.subject: cache
assumptions.statement: Balance cache hit-rate 85% on the balance-check path, so 15% of balance reads fall through to a read replica. Transfers always touch the cache for the idempotency key, never for the balance (the balance is re-read under lock from the primary).

assumptions.subject: db
assumptions.statement: One PostgreSQL WRITER for the ledger, sized at ~5,000 rps — lower than a plain OLTP primary because every posting is a multi-row double-entry transaction with a uniqueness constraint on the idempotency key. A Multi-AZ standby is assumed for failover; it is NOT modelled as extra capacity, because a synchronous standby serves no reads.

assumptions.subject: rep
assumptions.statement: Two async read replicas at ~6,000 rps each. History and cache-miss balance reads are served from them, so they are eventually consistent — a balance shown from a replica can lag a just-committed transfer by replication delay. Real wallets pin the post-transfer read to the primary; that pinning is not modelled.

assumptions.subject: scope
assumptions.statement: This is a CLOSED-LOOP wallet: balances move between accounts inside the ledger. External bank/card rails (ACH, card networks, mobile-money interconnect) are deliberately NOT modelled — they are third-party dependencies with no per-instance capacity or price, and Keystone would have to invent both. Model a rail separately as a rate-limited external dependency before trusting a top-up latency number.

assumptions.subject: q
assumptions.statement: 3-broker Kafka carrying post-commit events (push notification, settlement, fraud scoring) at ~3,000 msg/s. Sized for replication and broker-loss tolerance, not for throughput — utilisation is single-digit by design.

assumptions.subject: db
assumptions.statement: Ledger storage 4 TB on the primary and 4 TB per replica; the engine prices storage per COMPONENT, so the replica row carries 8 TB for the pair.

assumptions.subject: engine
assumptions.statement: Numbers here are steady-state peak-hour averages from an open queueing model. A wallet's real risk — a hot account row serialising concurrent transfers, or a payday spike an order of magnitude above peak — is a contention and burst problem the v1 analytical engine does not represent.

_library.summary: Consumer wallet with a double-entry ledger, cached balances, read replicas for history and an event bus for post-commit work.
